readerTitle: The milkshake that was hired for the commute
caseNote: 전해 내려오는 일화 (Clayton Christensen의 밀크셰이크 이야기, 체인 이름 비공개) + 가상 사례 (슈퍼마켓, 사내 교육팀)
insight: 고객은 제품을 사는 것이 아니라 특정 상황에서 나아가기 위해 제품을 '고용'한다. 그 상황을 알면 진짜 경쟁자와 고칠 점이 보인다.
misconception: 고객에게 제품을 어떻게 개선하면 좋을지 묻고, 요청받은 기능을 더하면 매출이 오른다. 경쟁자는 같은 종류의 제품뿐이다.

sources.text: Christensen, C. M., Cook, S., & Hall, T. (2005). Marketing Malpractice: The Cause and the Cure. Harvard Business Review.
Christensen, C. M., Hall, T., Dillon, K., & Duncan, D. S. (2016). Competing Against Luck. Harper Business.
슈퍼마켓, 사내 교육팀 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 밀크셰이크 이야기는 Christensen이 여러 강연과 글에서 반복해 전한 일화로, 판본마다 세부가 조금씩 다릅니다. 카드에는 'a story told by'와 'reportedly'로 일화임을 밝혔고, 7번 카드에서도 한계를 언급했습니다.
아침 판매 비중(판본에 따라 '약 40%' 또는 '거의 절반')은 출처마다 표현이 달라 카드에 수치를 넣지 않고 'many were sold early in the morning'으로만 적었습니다. 게시 전 HBR 2005 원문으로 확인하세요.
체인 이름은 원문에서 밝히지 않았으므로 카드에도 쓰지 않았습니다. 관찰한 연구자(Bob Moesta 등으로 알려짐)의 이름도 확인 전까지 쓰지 않았습니다.
설문 후 개선했으나 매출이 변하지 않았다는 점, 오후에 부모가 아이에게 사 주는 '두 번째 일'과 걸쭉한 셰이크가 오히려 문제가 된다는 점, 경쟁 대상(바나나, 베이글, 도넛)은 Competing Against Luck(2016)의 서술을 바탕으로 했습니다. 표현을 원문과 대조하세요.
'Jobs to be done' 용어는 Christensen이 대중화했지만 Tony Ulwick 등 다른 연구자의 기여도 있습니다. 그래서 카드에는 'invented'가 아니라 'popularized'로 적었습니다.
이 일화 이후 실제로 매출이 올랐는지는 공개 자료로 확인되지 않습니다. 카드에서 결과를 주장하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The milkshake that was hired for the commute
body: In a story Clayton Christensen often told, a fast-food chain wanted to sell more milkshakes. It asked customers how to make them better: thicker, cheaper, more chocolatey. It made the changes.
Sales barely moved. The answer came from watching who bought shakes early in the morning, and why.

image.label: A commuter driving at dawn with a milkshake in the cup holder
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 새벽 햇살 속 차 안, 운전자가 한 손으로 핸들을 잡고 컵홀더에 걸쭉한 밀크셰이크가 꽂혀 있음. 창밖으로 길게 이어진 도로. 실제 패스트푸드 브랜드 로고나 컵 디자인은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your shakes still aren't selling.
body: You manage a fast-food chain. Milkshake sales are flat. Customers in a survey asked for richer flavors and lower prices. You delivered both. Nothing changed.
What do you try next?

options.text: Run a bigger survey with more flavor ideas
options.feedback: You'd get more answers to the same question. The problem may be the question itself: it asks what people want from a shake, not why they buy one.

options.text: Watch who buys shakes, at what time, and what they do next
options.feedback: It's slower than a survey, but it shows the situation behind each purchase. That's where the chain in the story found its answer.

options.text: Cut the price again to test demand
options.feedback: Price matters, but you already tried it. Cheaper doesn't help much if the shake isn't doing what people bought it for.

cards.title: The shake's real rival was a banana.
body: A researcher reportedly spent long days in a restaurant, noting each shake sale. Many were sold early in the morning, to people alone, who drove off and drank them in the car.
Asked why, these commuters explained. They faced a long, dull drive. They wanted something to hold in one hand that lasted the whole trip and kept them full until lunch.
Bananas went too fast. Bagels were dry. Doughnuts left sticky fingers. A thick shake through a thin straw did the job best.

image.label: A milkshake competing against a banana, a bagel and a doughnut
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 가운데 'The morning commute' 라벨이 붙은 도로, 그 위에 밀크셰이크, 바나나, 베이글, 도넛이 후보처럼 나란히 서 있음. 각 아래에 짧은 메모: 'Gone in 2 minutes', 'Dry, crumbs', 'Sticky fingers', 'Lasts the drive'. 셰이크만 강조. 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Jobs to be done
body: **Jobs to be done** is the idea that people don't just buy products. They *hire* them to make progress in a particular situation.
The commuters' job wasn't "drink a milkshake." It was "make my boring drive bearable and stay full until lunch." Harvard professor Clayton Christensen popularized the idea.
Seen this way, your competition is anything else people could hire for the same job. For the shake, that included bananas and bagels.
cards.softwareNote: A small business may hire invoicing software for the job "get paid without awkward chasing." Its real rival might be a spreadsheet and a polite email, not another app with more features.

cards.title: Same product, different job.
body: In the story, the shake had a second job. In the afternoon, parents reportedly bought shakes for their kids as a small treat.
For them, a thick shake that takes ages to finish through a straw is a problem. They want it done before patience runs out.

That's why the survey failed. It averaged two jobs into one "typical customer" and got answers that fit neither. The morning job pointed to a thicker shake and faster buying. The afternoon job pointed to something smaller and quicker.

cards.title: The rotisserie chicken isn't competing with raw chicken.
body: A supermarket notices its hot roast chickens sell mostly between 5 and 7 p.m., to people still in work clothes.
The job: **get a hot dinner on the table within 15 minutes of walking in the door.** Their real rivals are pizza delivery and the drive-through, not the raw chicken in the meat aisle.
That changes the decisions. Put the chickens near the entrance, next to bagged salad and bread. Make sure the shelf is full at 5 p.m., not noon.

image.label: Hot roast chickens by a store entrance with salad and bread
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 슈퍼마켓 입구 바로 옆 진열대에 따뜻한 통닭구이, 봉지 샐러드, 빵이 한 세트로 놓여 있음. 퇴근 복장의 손님이 한 손에 가방을 들고 집어 가는 장면. 벽시계는 5:30. 실제 매장 로고 없음.

cards.title: A job that explains everything explains nothing.
body: "People want to feel happy" is technically a job, but it guides no decision. A useful job names the situation, the progress wanted, and what gets in the way.
Also remember that the milkshake story is a teaching story, retold many times, and details vary. Treat it as an illustration of the idea, not proof that thicker shakes sell.
Whatever job you think you've found, check it against what customers actually do, not just what they say.

cards.title: Now it's a team inside a company.
body: You run internal training at a 2,000-person company. Your online course for new managers gets good ratings, but few finish it. In feedback, managers ask for more topics.
What do you do?

options.text: Add the requested topics and more videos
options.feedback: You'd answer the request, but a longer course is even harder to finish. More content rarely fixes a product hired for the wrong job.

options.text: Find the moments new managers look for help, like the night before a first hard conversation, and build short guides for those
options.feedback: You give up a neat, complete curriculum. You gain something managers actually reach for when the job shows up.
Completion goes up, but you'd be measuring attendance, not help. People will click through just to get it done.

cards.title: Ask what job your product was hired to do.
body: Customers hire products to make progress in a specific situation. Find the situation, and you'll see your real rivals and what to improve.
**Try it today:** ask three recent customers, "What were you doing just before you bought from us, and what would you have used instead?"
